items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: saying that he and his Dick Welstood were having what he described as a very delicate conversation

ctx.x: country, and that's the way I felt then and that's the way I feel now. But on the other hand, I don't go as far to the right as George Brunis did which, he read the Chicago American, and that was the extent of his political beliefs. I'm not that naive, for me, to think that way. There's a lot of things wrong.

Kenny was talking about Brunis the other night, saying that he and his Dick Welstood were having what he described as a very delicate conversation wherein the Cuban crisis -- and everybody in New York, those missiles were going to be sent out. And he said, Brunis just barged in and heard what they were talking about and said, drop a bomb on and that'll stop all that shit.

It was common talk. I'm not saying anything about George that hasn't been talked by all musicians. Everybody who knew George knew that the extent of his reading matter, probably, was the Chicago American, it was easy to read, they had some good jokes there, a puzzle and things like that. And plus, he didn't have a great deal of education and that was it.
